question: What kind of tissue lines the inside of your oesophagus to protect it from rough food?

options.B: Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells

explanation: Great job! Because swallowing food creates a lot of friction, the oesophagus needs a tough, multi-layered lining (stratified squamous) to keep underlying tissues safe. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h1)

question: How does the muscle type in the oesophagus change from the top down?

options.A: It remains entirely composed of involuntary smooth muscle.
options.B: It shifts from skeletal muscle to smooth muscle.
options.C: It shifts from smooth muscle to skeletal muscle.
options.D: It remains entirely composed of skeletal muscle fibers.

explanation: You've got this! The top part is skeletal muscle (under our conscious control for swallowing), while the lower two-thirds shift to smooth muscle to automatically push food down. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h1)

question: Where is the very first narrowing or constriction found in the oesophagus?
explanation: Spot on! The uppermost narrowing is right at the start of the oesophagus, formed by a muscle called the cricopharyngeus. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h2)

question: Why might a patient with an enlarged heart (specifically an enlarged left atrium) find it hard to swallow?

options.A: The atrium presses directly against the anterior wall of the adjacent oesophagus.
options.B: Compression shuts down the vagus nerve endings supplying the stomach.
options.C: The heart enlargement blocks blood flow through the surrounding thoracic duct.
options.D: The diaphragm is pushed upward and prevents the lower sphincter from opening.

explanation: Makes total sense when you picture it: the left atrium sits right in front of the middle of the oesophagus, so if the heart swells, it pushes against the food pipe and narrows it! [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h2)

question: Why are the veins in the lower part of the oesophagus so critical during liver disease?

options.A: They prevent stomach acid from washing backward into the throat.
options.B: They supply the main nerve impulses that trigger swallowing waves.
options.C: They carry all arterial blood returning from the entire stomach.
options.D: They form a direct connection between portal and systemic veins.

explanation: Well done! Because these veins link the liver's portal system to the general body circulation, they can bulge and bleed dangerously when liver scarring blocks blood flow. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which artery provides the main blood supply to the abdominal section of the oesophagus?
explanation: You're learning fast! As the oesophagus drops down into the belly area, it picks up its blood supply mostly from branches of the left gastric artery. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which cranial nerve is mainly responsible for controlling the muscles of the oesophagus?
explanation: Correct! The vagus nerve is the major highway for signals that coordinate those smooth swallowing contractions. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h4)

question: What normally kicks off a 'secondary' wave of movement (peristalsis) in the oesophagus?

options.A: Distension of the oesophageal wall by a trapped food bolus
options.B: Relaxation of the lower sphincter caused by stomach acid
options.C: Sympathetic stimulation from the thoracic chain ganglia
options.D: Direct voluntary signals sent from the cerebral cortex

explanation: Spot on! If a piece of food gets stuck or stretches the wall, local nerves trigger a secondary squeeze to clear out whatever the first wave left behind. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the main job of the upper oesophageal sphincter when you are just resting and not swallowing?

options.A: To stop gastric acid from reaching the pharynx
options.B: To prevent air from entering the digestive tract
options.C: To produce mucus for lubricating food boluses
options.D: To grind up large food particles before entry

explanation: Great thinking! By staying shut when we aren't eating, this sphincter keeps us from accidentally sucking air into our stomach every time we breathe in. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h5)

question: How does the lower oesophageal sphincter keep itself tightly closed to stop acid reflux?

options.A: By active mucus production sealing the lower mucosal folds together
options.B: Through intrinsic smooth muscle tone reinforced by the diaphragmatic crura
options.C: By voluntary contraction of skeletal muscle fibers wrapped around the hiatus
options.D: Through continuous parasympathetic stimulation sent by the glossopharyngeal nerve

explanation: You got it! It relies on its own natural muscle tension plus a helpful extra squeeze from the diaphragm opening it passes through. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h5)

question: What are the two major muscle problems seen in a patient with achalasia?

options.A: Premature contraction of the diaphragm and paralysis of the phrenic nerve
options.B: Weakness of the upper sphincter and rapid food transit into the duodenum
options.C: Constant spasm of the upper sphincter and excessive stomach acid production
options.D: Failure of the lower sphincter to relax and lack of normal peristalsis

explanation: Brilliant! In achalasia, the food pipe forgets how to push food down properly (no peristalsis), and the bottom valve stubbornly stays clamped shut. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which of these conditions is NOT typically linked to portal hypertension in the liver?
explanation: Spot on! Achalasia is a nerve and muscle issue of the oesophagus itself, completely separate from high blood pressure in the liver circulation. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T2#GNS121_U1_T2_h6)
